paragraphs.source_en: There is another case in which something can be exposed even without making a sound. Once, long ago, when I went to the hot springs at Ubako, I shared a room with an old man, apparently the retired proprietor of some Tokyo dry-goods shop. Well, since we were simply sharing lodgings, it made no difference to me whether he sold silk goods or old clothes. But one troublesome thing did happen. On the third day after I arrived at Ubako, I ran out of tobacco. As you probably know, Ubako is a lone inn deep in the mountains, an inconvenient place where there is nothing much to do except bathe in the hot spring and eat. So to run out of tobacco there was a real calamity. Once a thing is gone, one wants it all the more; the moment I thought I had no tobacco, though I am usually not such a heavy smoker, I suddenly longed desperately for a smoke. And to make matters worse, that old man had come up the mountain with a whole bundle packed full of tobacco. He would take it out little by little, sit cross-legged in front of me, and puff away as if to say, Well? You want some too, don't you? If he had merely smoked in front of me, I might have endured it, but at last he began blowing smoke rings, blowing them upright, blowing them sideways, even blowing them in reverse like the pillow in the dream of Handan, and sometimes sending the smoke in and out through his nostrils. In short, he was smoking for show.
